elements.text: verl reward verifiers — how they work
Every way verl turns a model's answer into a number it can learn from: rule-based scorers, code sandboxes, reward models, and the machinery around them
Read from RL/verl-main. New to RL? Start with page 1. Every box with a page number jumps there (click in view mode, Ctrl+click while editing; Alt+← comes back).

In plain words
The model writes an answer. A verifier checks it against the known right answer and gives back a score — usually 1 for right and 0 for wrong. Training then nudges the model toward answers that scored higher. This drawing explains every verifier verl ships and how the score travels from the checker to the trainer.

Two families of reward managers
Current: verl/experimental/reward_loop/ — async, run by RewardLoopWorker Ray actors while rollouts are still generating. This is what the PPO trainer uses today.
Legacy: verl/workers/reward_manager/ — synchronous, still exported and tested, but the trainer no longer wires them.
Not here: there is no IFEval scorer in verl's reward_score package. math_verify, rlla and subEM exist but are only reachable through a custom reward function.

What a reward is, what the trainer does with it, and what a dataset row must contain

In plain words
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) works like a teacher grading homework with an answer key. The model tries a question several times, each try gets a grade, and the model is pushed toward the tries that did better than its own average.
GRPO in one picture — one question, 4 tries

mean = 0.25, std = 0.5 (torch.std, unbiased) → the right try gets +1.5, the wrong ones −0.5. Every token of a try is pushed up or down by its advantage. If all 4 tries got the same reward, every advantage is 0 and nothing is learned from that question — which is why a verifier that is too strict or too lenient both hurt.
Where the reward sits: on the last token

The verifier returns one number per response. verl writes it at the position of the last valid (non-padding) response token and puts 0 everywhere else — an "outcome reward". GRPO sums over tokens, so the sum is just the score.

Rule-based (the default)
A Python function compares the answer with ground_truth: regexes, string cleanup, sympy, or running code. Cheap, deterministic, but only works when there is a checkable answer.

Model-based
Another LLM (a reward model) reads the prompt and answer and outputs a score. A discriminative RM returns a number directly; a generative RM (GenRM) writes a judgement your custom function parses. Turned on with reward.reward_model.enable.
Anatomy of a dataset row (made by examples/data_preprocess/*.py)

Three things matter for rewards
• data_source picks the scorer (exact string match).
• reward_model.ground_truth is the answer key — its format depends on the scorer: a number string, a \boxed{} content, a dict {"target": [...]}, or JSON test cases.
• The prompt must ask for the answer in the format the scorer extracts ("####", \boxed{}, <answer>…).
default_compute_score(data_source, solution_str, ground_truth, …) — one if/elif chain that picks the scorer

In plain words
Like a mail sorter: it reads the label on each row (data_source) and hands the answer to the right checker. An unknown label is an error, not a zero.
sandbox_fusion if a URL is set, else prime_code  →  page 7
unchanged — must have "score"; other keys → reward_extra_info

Gotchas
• extra_info and **kwargs are accepted but never passed to any scorer.
• "AIME2024" or "math/aime" don't match startswith("aime") — examples/rewards/custome_reward_fn/aime_reward.py remaps the tag for exactly this reason.
• math_verify, rlla and search_r1's subEM are never routed: use a custom reward function (page 12).

In plain words
Grade-school word problems. The prompt tells the model to finish with "#### <number>". The checker finds the last such number and compares it with the answer key letter by letter.

take the LAST match
remove , and $

1.0 if equal
0.0 (format_score) if not
0 if nothing found

Ground truth: examples/data_preprocess/gsm8k.py takes the text after "#### " in the reference answer and removes commas → "72", "1234". Prompt suffix: Let's think step by step and output the final answer after "####".
strict vs flexible: the dispatcher always uses strict. flexible takes the last number anywhere (that isn't "" or "."), so "the answer is 1234" passes — only if you call gsm8k yourself.
the regex needs a digit right after "#### " → nothing

Gotchas
• No numeric comparison: "72.0" ≠ "72".
• docs/preparation/reward_function.rst promises 0.1 for correct format, but format_score defaults to 0.0 and the dispatcher never passes it.
• The 300-char clip means a "####" earlier in a long answer is never seen.
math_reward.compute_score(solution_str, ground_truth) — the lm-eval-harness Hendrycks MATH check

In plain words
Competition math. The model puts its final answer in \boxed{…}. The checker pulls out the last box, tidies up the LaTeX on both sides with a fixed list of rules, and compares the two strings.
strip_string — the cleanup rules, in order

Gotchas
• Pure string comparison after cleanup — 0.25 vs \frac14 fails; only 0.5 is special-cased.
• Two "\text{ " pieces make remove_right_units assert; is_equiv catches it and compares the raw strings.
• No dependencies at all — fast and predictable.

Ground truth: examples/data_preprocess/math_dataset.py stores remove_boxed(last_boxed_only_string(solution)) — the content of the reference solution's last box. Prompt suffix: Let's think step by step and output the final answer within \boxed{}.

In plain words
Used for DAPO-Math-17k and AIME. It looks for a line starting "Answer:", cleans it up, and compares. Note the scale: a right answer is +1 and a wrong one is −1, not 0.

fallback: is_correct_strict_box
last 100 chars → last \boxed{} → RAW == gt (no normalization)
strict_box_verify=True skips the "Answer:" step and uses only the box check.

1. keep what follows the last "="
x = 5  →  5

3. REMOVED_EXPRESSIONS
units and words: square, ways, dollars, mph, inches, hours, km, points, feet, degrees, cm, … \ldots, ^\circ, {,}

6. strip $; drop commas from pure numbers; strip()
1,000 → 1000

Gotchas
• Scores are +1 / −1. Mixing math_dapo rows with 0/1 scorers in one run mixes reward scales (page 13).
• The "a " / "an " substitutions also hit inside words ("banana " loses an "a ").
• In the box fallback the ground truth is not normalized — a raw == compare.
• verify() is annotated -> bool but returns a tuple.
prime_math.compute_score(model_output, ground_truth) → (is_correct, format_correctness, extracted) — for the numina_* sources

In plain words
The most forgiving rule-based math checker in verl. It guesses where the answer is from phrases like "the answer is", then tries string cleanup, then sympy, then numeric closeness — any one of them saying "equal" is enough.
before the last "is answer" / "is the answer" / "are the answers"

_normalize: unwrap \text{}, drop % and $, " or "/" and " → ",", million → *10^6, units (degree, cm, meter, mile, hour, …), \circ, LaTeX → text (√ → sqrt, π → pi), "7 3/4" → "7+3/4", lowercase — equal?

split tuples / intervals: bracket types and counts must match, then per element: both fractions → exact string only; integer-ness differs → no; else sympy simplify(gt − pred) == 0 (10 s timeout, ≤ 2 unknown letters)
math_equal fallback: numbers isclose(rel_tol 1e-4) against ref/100, ref, ref·100 (percent forms), intervals, tuples, Point(…), matrices; \pi tried as math.pi and 3.14
symbolic_equal — always False because of a bug (below)
First three asserted in tests/utils/reward_score/test_sandbox_on_cpu.py; the 50% case traced by hand.

Bug: grader.py uses timeout_limit as a context manager (with timeout_limit(seconds=…):), but verl/utils/py_functional.py defines it as a decorator. The with-statement raises TypeError, the broad except swallows it, and symbolic_equal always returns False — the last fallback is dead code. (grade_answer's sympy step uses the decorator correctly and still works.)
Also: eval() on strings derived from model output (handle_pi, the matrix branch).

format_correctness = "Step 2:" in output and "\box" in output — returned, but the dispatcher keeps only res[0], so it never affects the reward. Dependencies: sympy, pylatexenc; sympy calls run in a fresh process (timeout_limit) for 10 s.
For codecontests / apps / codeforces / taco: run the model's program on test cases and score the pass rate

In plain words
For coding problems the verifier actually runs the program. Each test case gives an input and the expected output; the score is the fraction of tests passed (looking at the first 10). Two engines exist: run it locally (prime_code) or send it to a SandboxFusion server.

sandbox_fusion.compute_score
HTTP to a remote sandbox

prime_code.compute_score
runs locally in a child process
split on ```python … ```; pure code without a fence is accepted
needs a code fence — no fence → 0.0 "missing code block"
multiprocessing.Process + signal.alarm per case; reliability_guard() disables exit/os/shutil — "NOT a security sandbox"
POST {code, stdin, compile_timeout, run_timeout, memory_limit_MB, language} to the URL; 29 languages; retries only on HTTP 504 (×3)
5 s for the all-cases pass, 10 s per case
compile/run 10 s; request timeout = compile + run + 10
all pass → 1.0; else first 10 cases one by one → passed / run
continuous: passed in the first min(n, 10) / that count
Continuous scoring — only the first 10 cases count
11 test cases, first 9 pass → 9 / 10 = 0.9  (asserted in tests/utils/reward_score/test_sandbox_on_cpu.py: prime_code_scores = [1.0, 0.9])
didn't compile; later cases marked -4 too
the service failed, not the code

Gotchas
• The same completion can score differently depending on whether a sandbox URL is set (code fence rule).
• prime_code.compute_score(continuous=False) raises UnboundLocalError when not every test passes (the dispatcher always passes continuous=True).
• A custom reward function turns off the automatic sandbox wiring (page 12).
• prime_code runs model code on the reward worker host.
Two scorers with small twists: a format bonus, and exact-match QA with a spam guard

In plain words
Geometry3K gives most of the credit for the right answer and a little (0.1) for using the requested layout. Search-R1 checks a short text answer inside <answer> tags after light cleanup (lowercase, no punctuation, no "a/an/the").

format = 1.0 if re.fullmatch(r"<think>.*</think>.*\\boxed\{.*\}.*", s, DOTALL) else 0.0
acc    = 1.0 if mathruler.grade_answer(extract_boxed_content(s), gt) else 0.0
score  = 0.9 * acc + 0.1 * format

Possible values: 0.0, 0.1, 0.9, 1.0 (traced from the code; mathruler not installed here). Gotcha: if the chat template treats <think> as a special token, decoding with skip_special_tokens=True drops the tags and silently loses the 0.1.
normalize: lowercase, drop punctuation, drop a/an/the, squash spaces

EM: equal to any target
(subEM: contains one)

Ground truth is a dict: {"target": ["golden answer", "another"]}. preprocess_search_r1_dataset.py sets data_source = "searchR1_" + the original source. If the answer matches but <answer> or </answer> appears more than 10 times, the score is cut to 0.25 (anti tag-spam). Prints debug output with probability 1/64.
Two scorers you can only reach through a custom reward function: HF math-verify, and the RLLA tool-call reward

In plain words
math-verify is a library that understands math answers properly (fractions, decimals, expressions). The tool-call reward grades whether the model called the right tools with the right arguments, plus a bonus for the expected layout.
send to a spawned ProcessPool(4) — signal.alarm works there

any verify(g, p) → 1.0
else 0.0; 30 s timeout → 0

Use it via a custom function (tests/experimental/reward_loop/reward_fn.py::compute_score_math_verify) with reward.reward_manager.name=remote, so it runs in separate Ray processes — the remote manager exists because math-verify misbehaves in thread pools (verl issue #3407). Example: "x = \frac{1}{2}" vs gt "0.5" should score 1.0 (symbolic/numeric equivalence; not run here). Gotcha: a timed-out future isn't cancelled, so slow jobs can occupy all 4 workers.
rlla.compute_score — tool-call reward (used by the GDPO example)

ground truth:  <tool_call>\n{"name": "get_weather", "parameters": {"city": "Paris"}}\n</tool_call>
expected form: <think>…</think>\n<tool_call>\n…\n</tool_call>   (+ <response>…</response>)

format   ∈ {0, 1}    one regex per case; each tag exactly once
accuracy ∈ [−3, 3]   no gt tool → 0 · unparsable → −3 · exact list → 3
                     else 6 · score / local_max − 3
returns  {score: format + accuracy, format_reward, accuracy_reward}

Lyon case, by hand: names match (1) + keys match (1) + values 0 = 2; local_max = 1 + (1 + 1 param) = 3; accuracy = 6·2/3 − 3 = 1.0. Partial credit is graded, unlike every math scorer. Needs extra_info["experiment_name"] containing "qwen" or "llama" — the gdpo manager injects it.

How the GDPO example wires it: reward.custom_reward_function.path=…/rlla.py, reward.reward_manager.name=gdpo, +algorithm.gdpo_reward_keys='["accuracy_reward","format_reward"]' (examples/gdpo_trainer/run_qwen3_8b_fsdp.sh) — GDPO normalizes each reward component separately using those extra-info keys.
The wrappers around the scorers — and the RewardLoopWorker that runs them, rule-based or with a reward model

In plain words
A reward manager is the clerk: it turns token ids back into text, looks up the answer key, calls the scorer, adds any penalty, and hands back the score plus extra info. Several of them run in parallel as Ray workers while the model is still generating.
run_single(one sample) — what every current manager does
3. data_source = non_tensor_batch["data_source"] · ground_truth = ["reward_model"]["ground_truth"] · extra_info (+ num_turns, tool_extra_fields, rollout_reward_scores)
4. await compute_score(...) if async, else run it in the default thread pool
5. dict result → score = result["score"], every key → reward_extra_info; scalar → reward_extra_info["acc"] = score
the default — exactly the five steps
runs compute_score in separate Ray CPU actors, round-robin; no async functions — for heavy or thread-unsafe scorers
semaphore + requests/tokens-per-minute buckets + timeout (default 300 s) — for paid APIs; timeout/error → 0.0
Pick with reward.reward_manager.name. Legacy batch / prime exist in verl/workers/reward_manager/ but can't be selected by name anymore.
DAPO overlong penalty — too-long answers lose reward

expected_len    = max_resp_len − overlong_buffer.len
exceed_len      = valid_response_length − expected_len
overlong_reward = min(−exceed_len / overlong_buffer.len · penalty_factor, 0)
reward         += overlong_reward

Enable with +reward.reward_kwargs.overlong_buffer_cfg.{enable, len, penalty_factor, log} and +reward.reward_kwargs.max_resp_len. Test (test_dapo_on_cpu.py): max 4, buffer 2, length 4 → penalty −1.0, so 0.5 becomes −0.5.
penalty vs response length (max 20480, buffer 4096, factor 1)

Reward models
RewardModelManager launches vLLM / SGLang servers for reward.reward_model.model_path behind an HTTP router, colocated with the actor (woken and slept around scoring) or in their own pool (reward.reward_model.enable_resource_pool), which lets scores stream during rollout.
GenRM: write an async custom function that POSTs to http://{reward_router_address}/v1/chat/completions and parses the judge's reply — tests/experimental/reward_loop/reward_fn.py::compute_score_gsm8k asks for a 1–10 grade and returns {score, acc: score == 10, genrm_response}.
From a finished rollout to the advantages — who calls what, and what shape the data has at each step

In plain words
Scoring happens while other answers are still being generated: as soon as one trajectory finishes, it is sent to a reward worker. When the whole batch is assembled, the scores become a tensor that the trainer turns into advantages.
trajectory done → _compute_score: 1-sample DataProto (prompts, responses, mask, data_source, reward_model, extra_info)
compute_score: pick a path (custom / RM / rules)
run_single: decode, read ground_truth, call scorer
batch assembled: rm_scores[i, last token] = score; extra keys → non_tensor_batch
extract_reward → token_level_scores → (−KL if use_kl_in_reward) → token_level_rewards → advantages
One task per finished trajectory, sent to a randomly chosen worker (reward.num_workers, default 8). Colocated reward models instead score the whole batch later via RewardLoopManager.compute_rm_score.
rm_scores  [batch = 2, response_len = 8]   (blue = real tokens, grey = padding)

Gotcha: the extra-info keys are taken from the first sample only, then read for every sample. If samples return different dict keys (rate_limited adds "timeout" only on timeouts), assembling the batch raises KeyError. Keep your dict keys identical for every sample.
The reward.* config tree, and how to plug in your own reward function

In plain words
You rarely edit verl's scorers. Either your dataset uses a data_source the dispatcher knows, or you point reward.custom_reward_function.path at a small Python file of your own.
register, or importlib with module.path / name
extra kwargs on every call (override call kwargs)
own GPUs for the RM → streaming scores

Old top-level keys (custom_reward_function.*, reward_model.*, sandbox_fusion.*) live in legacy_reward_impl.yaml;
migrate_legacy_reward_impl copies them over — it is only called from the fully-async entrypoint as far as the reading found.

Rules of thumb
• Called with keyword arguments; keep **kwargs (an RM router adds reward_router_address, reward_model_tokenizer).
• Return a float, or a dict with "score" — same keys for every sample.
• async def is allowed (not with the remote manager).
• To reuse the built-ins, call default_compute_score yourself (see examples/rewards/custome_reward_fn/aime_reward.py).
• Setting a custom function disables the automatic sandbox_fusion wiring.

Other ways to customize
• Heavy or thread-unsafe scorer → reward.reward_manager.name=remote.
• Paid API judge → rate_limited with +reward.max_rpm / max_tpm / timeout.
• Your own manager class → source=importlib, module.path=/file.py, name=MyManager (subclass RewardManagerBase, implement async run_single), or @register("myname").
• The dataset must provide data_source and reward_model.ground_truth; a discriminative RM also needs raw_prompt (data.return_raw_chat=True).
Every scorer's possible scores on one number line, timeouts, and the bugs worth knowing

In plain words
Scorers don't agree on a scale. Most give 0 or 1, DAPO math gives −1 or +1, code gives a fraction, and the tool-call reward goes from −3 to 4. If one training run mixes datasets, these scales mix too.
RewardLoopWorker actors + an asyncio task per sample
aiohttp, 16 retries, backoff up to 30 s
1. prime_math symbolic_equal always False (decorator used as a context manager)
2. prime_code continuous=False → UnboundLocalError on any failure
3. extra-info keys from the first sample only → KeyError if dicts differ
4. math_dapo is ±1 while most scorers are 0/1
5. gsm8k: docs promise a 0.1 format score; code gives 0.0; "72." ≠ "72"
6. sandbox_fusion needs a code fence; prime_code doesn't
7. a custom reward function disables the sandbox_fusion wiring
8. reward-loop managers hard-code "data_source" and don't print num_examine samples
9. default_compute_score ignores extra_info; "aime" is a case-sensitive prefix
10. legacy prime manager zeroes the whole batch on a dict-returning scorer
11. no IFEval scorer in this repo
